title: Affinity, Spillover, and Regional Routing Playbook
content:
Purpose and scope:

This doc codifies pragmatic routing patterns we use across Redwood deployments (Hosted, Dedicated, Private) focused on: affinity (strong/soft), spillover/fallback, and region-aware decisions. It is intended for platform engineers implementing control-plane routing logic and edge/data-plane proxy owners.

Goals:
- Give clear routing primitives that map to business constraints (isolation, latency SLOs, cost caps).
- Surface trade-offs for each deployment mode and recommend safe defaults.
- Provide operational runbooks for common failure modes (region outage, capacity exhaustion, control plane partition).

Key terminology (short):
- Control plane: global/regional service(s) that make placement/routing decisions (not where inference executes).
- Data plane: proxies, local routers, and inference nodes that carry requests and execute models.
- Strong affinity: requests from a tenant are pinned to a particular pool/region/instance for consistency/isolation (no automatic spillover).
- Soft affinity: routing favors a preferred pool/region but allows controlled spillover when capacity is lacking or for latency optimization.
- Spillover (fallback): policy that re-routes requests to a secondary target when primary target is unavailable/capped.
- Tenant isolation boundary: the set of mechanisms (network, compute, KMS, auditing) that enforce separation across tenants.

High-level decision matrix (one-liner):
- Hosted: prioritize latency and availability with multi-region soft-affinity and automated spillover; isolation via logical separation + strict telemetry and per-tenant RBAC.
- Dedicated: prioritize predictability/isolation with strong affinity to reserved GPU pools and limited controlled spillover only under explicit administrative policy.
- Private: prioritize customer isolation and network controls with local control plane placements and affinity decided by customer config (default strong).

Routing primitives and when to use them:
1) Strong affinity (pin-to-pool/region)
   - Use for: Dedicated customers with reserved capacity, PII/regulatory workloads, or customers with explicit contractual isolation.
   - Behavioral contract: no automatic cross-boundary routing. If capacity exhausted, requests fail or are queued.
   - Enforcement: tenant tags in control plane, routing table entries, and admission control at local router.

2) Soft affinity (prefer-local then spillover)
   - Use for: Hosted tenants and workloads that tolerate model variant fallbacks for availability/cost.
   - Behavioral contract: prefer nearest/preferred pool; on saturation (or degraded latency) fall back to secondary pool that preserves isolation level required by tenant.
   - Enforcement: weighted routing keys, token metadata containing isolation requirements, and staged fallbacks (same-region -> adjacent-region -> global fallback).

3) Region-first routing
   - Use for: latency-critical but non-sensitive workloads. Prioritize region-local pools even if slightly more expensive.

4) Cost-priority routing
   - Use for: low-cost tiers or best-effort batch requests. Control plane picks cheaper quantized/FP16 model variant potentially in a different region.

Interaction with model variants and quality guarantees:
- Routing decisions should carry a "quality budget" tag. Control plane only routes to lower-quality variants when the tag indicates tolerance. This prevents silent quality regressions during spillover.

Control plane architectures (trade-offs):
A) Centralized global control plane
   - Pros: single source of truth, simpler global policies, easier rollout coordination.
   - Cons: higher blast radius on failure, increased egress for telemetry, potential latency for per-request route queries.
   - Best fit: Hosted where we can tolerate a global control plane and want uniform policy.

B) Regional control planes with global coordination
   - Pros: lower routing decision latency, regionally autonomous during partial partitions, smaller failure blast radius.
   - Cons: increased complexity for global policy sync and cross-region consistency.
   - Best fit: Multi-region Hosted and Dedicated where customers have regional residency requirements.

C) Customer-local control plane (Private)
   - Pros: full customer control, no outbound control plane egress, supports air-gapped deployments.
   - Cons: operator burden on customer, harder to provide cross-customer features.

Recommended control plane pattern by deployment mode:
- Hosted: global control plane + regional caches at edge proxies. Control plane issues per-request hints (preferred pool id, allowed fallbacks, quality budget). Edge keeps a short-lived routing cache and enforces local admission.
- Dedicated: regional or pool-local control plane primarily authoritative. Global control plane exists for catalog/versioning but not for per-request routing unless explicitly configured.
- Private: allow customer-managed control plane; provide optional operator sync hooks (audit-only) to help with upgrades. Defaults to strong affinity.

Data plane routing behavior:
- Edge proxies consult local cache for routing decisions. Fall back to control plane only when cache miss or policy change (avoid per-request control plane hop).
- Admission control at data plane: enforce per-tenant concurrency budgets, per-route qps, and model-level rate limits.
- Telemetry: always attach origin, preferred-pool, actual-pool, model-variant, and quality-budget to traces for postmortem and quality monitoring.

Isolation boundary mapping (controls):
- Network: VPCs, subnet segmentation, and egress filtering (strong for Dedicated/Private).
- Compute: GPU pools tagged and reserved for tenant or colocated logical namespaces.
- Storage: encryption keys scoped per-tenant; Private/Dedicated default to per-tenant KMS.
- Audit/Logs: separate retention and access controls for Dedicated/Private. Hosted uses strict multi-tenant ACLs.

Failure modes and mitigations (short):
- Capacity exhaustion in preferred pool: soft affinity -> spillover (Hosted); Dedicated -> queue/fail and trigger autoscale/alert to SRE.
- Region partition: regional control plane mode -> operate autonomously using last-known routing state; global mode -> edge falls back to cached policies and switch to alternate region if allowed.
- Control plane full outage: edges operate in read-only cached mode for a graceful window; if the cache expires, block new requests depending on tenant isolation level and configured fallback.

Operational runbooks (summary):
- Runbook 1: Preferred pool saturation (Hosted). Steps: detect saturation -> enable spillover to adjacent region -> monitor quality signals -> if quality drops, throttle non-critical customers and/or spin up additional capacity for critical tenants.
- Runbook 2: Dedicated pool overcommit due to noisy neighbor. Steps: identify offending workloads -> enforce per-tenant floor limits -> evict or throttle as contractual policy, engage SE for customer communication.
- Runbook 3: Control plane partition. Steps: switch edge caches to cached policy, disable non-essential rollouts, notify customers who rely on global decisions for isolation.

Rollout and testing guidance:
- Canary fallbacks: test spillover targets with synthetic load and holdout test tenants to detect regressions.
- Chaos testing: simulate region loss and validate read-only cache behavior for at least 30 minutes.
- Eval-driven quality alarms: link routing-induced variant changes to eval suites so spillover that materially changes outputs triggers an SLO alert.

Recommended defaults (short):
- Hosted: soft-affinity, multi-region spillover enabled, quality-budget default = "preserve-model-variant" for paid tiers and "allow-quantized-fallback" for free/low tiers.
- Dedicated: strong-affinity by default, operator override for controlled spillover, per-tenant KMS.
- Private: respect customer-specified affinity; default to strong.

Outstanding decisions and follow-ups:
- Define exact TTL for edge routing cache vs expected control-plane churn (proposal: 30s default, configurable by tenant).
- Standardize "quality-budget" tokens and policy enforcement points.
- Contract language for Dedicated spillover behavior to include explicit approval gates.

Appendix: quick checklist for implementing a new routing policy
- Define isolation guarantee required by tenant (none/soft/strong).
- Decide control plane authority (global/regional/local).
- Map allowed spillover targets and model variants for each tenant class.
- Add telemetry hooks and eval linkages.
- Create canary and chaos plans.

This is an operational playbook draft — feedback welcome.

Notes to reviewers:
- If you are implementing edge code, focus on cache semantics and admission control hooks.
- If you are implementing control plane, prioritize compact, signed routing tokens that edges can verify without contacting the CP on every request.
- For security/compliance owners: review the KMS and network mapping sections and mark any customers that require stricter defaults.
